claim: At Caenorhabditis elegans neuromuscular junctions, CaV2 and CaV1 voltage-gated calcium channels mediate the release of distinct pools of synaptic vesicles.
source: We demonstrate that at Caenorhabditis elegans neuromuscular junctions two different classes of voltage-gated calcium channels, CaV2 and CaV1, mediate the release of distinct pools of synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental approaches including electrophysiology, electron microscopy, and super-resolution imaging presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: CaV2 channels are concentrated in densely packed clusters approximately 250 nm in diameter.
source: CaV2 channels are concentrated in densely packed clusters ~250 nm in diameter with the active zone proteins Neurexin, α-Liprin, SYDE, ELKS/CAST, RIM-BP, α-Catulin, and MAGI1.
evidence: This is supported by super-resolution microscopy data showing CaV2 cluster dimensions.

claim: CaV2 channels colocalize with active zone proteins including Neurexin, α-Liprin, SYDE, ELKS/CAST, RIM-BP, α-Catulin, and MAGI1.
source: CaV2 channels are concentrated in densely packed clusters ~250 nm in diameter with the active zone proteins Neurexin, α-Liprin, SYDE, ELKS/CAST, RIM-BP, α-Catulin, and MAGI1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution imaging showing colocalization of CaV2 with these proteins.

claim: CaV2 channels are colocalized with the priming protein UNC-13L.
source: CaV2 channels are colocalized with the priming protein UNC-13L and mediate the fusion of vesicles docked within 33 nm of the dense projection.
evidence: This is supported by super-resolution microscopy data showing spatial association between CaV2 and UNC-13L.

claim: CaV2 channels mediate the fusion of vesicles docked within 33 nm of the dense projection.
source: CaV2 channels are colocalized with the priming protein UNC-13L and mediate the fusion of vesicles docked within 33 nm of the dense projection.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flash-and-freeze electron microscopy showing vesicle fusion patterns in CaV2 mutants.

claim: CaV2 activity is amplified by ryanodine receptor release of calcium from internal stores.
source: CaV2 activity is amplified by ryanodine receptor release of calcium from internal stores, triggering fusion up to 165 nm from the dense projection.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology showing reduced multiquantal release when RyR is blocked, and electron microscopy showing fusion patterns.

claim: Ryanodine receptor activation by CaV2 triggers vesicle fusion up to 165 nm from the dense projection.
source: CaV2 activity is amplified by ryanodine receptor release of calcium from internal stores, triggering fusion up to 165 nm from the dense projection.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flash-and-freeze electron microscopy showing fusion patterns in the intermediate active zone.

claim: CaV1 channels are dispersed in the synaptic varicosity.
source: By contrast, CaV1 channels are dispersed in the synaptic varicosity, and are colocalized with UNC-13S.
evidence: This is supported by super-resolution microscopy showing broad distribution of CaV1 localizations.

claim: CaV1 channels are colocalized with UNC-13S.
source: By contrast, CaV1 channels are dispersed in the synaptic varicosity, and are colocalized with UNC-13S.
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution microscopy showing spatial association between CaV1 and UNC-13S.

claim: CaV1 and ryanodine receptors are separated by approximately 40 nm.
source: CaV1 and ryanodine receptors are separated by just 40 nm, and vesicle fusion mediated by CaV1 is completely dependent on the ryanodine receptor.
evidence: This is supported by nearest neighbor analysis from super-resolution microscopy data.

claim: Vesicle fusion mediated by CaV1 is completely dependent on the ryanodine receptor.
source: CaV1 and ryanodine receptors are separated by just 40 nm, and vesicle fusion mediated by CaV1 is completely dependent on the ryanodine receptor.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology showing that blocking RyR eliminates CaV1-mediated vesicle fusion, and electron microscopy showing no lateral vesicle fusion in RyR mutants.

claim: The CaV1 CaV2 double mutant is synthetic lethal.
source: However, CaV1(Δns) CaV2(-) double mutants and RyR(-) CaV2(-) double mutants exhibit a synthetic lethal interaction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by viability assays showing that the double mutant cannot survive.

claim: The RyR CaV2 double mutant is synthetic lethal.
source: However, CaV1(Δns) CaV2(-) double mutants and RyR(-) CaV2(-) double mutants exhibit a synthetic lethal interaction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by viability assays showing that the double mutant cannot survive.

claim: The CaV1(Δns) RyR(-) double mutant is viable.
source: The double mutant CaV1(Δns) RyR(-) is viable, and is no worse than the RyR null, consistent with their coupled function (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by viability assays.

claim: Calcium influx from CaV1-RyR acts redundantly and in parallel with CaV2 to sustain neuronal function essential for viability.
source: These data suggest that calcium influx from CaV1-RyR acts redundantly, and in parallel, with CaV2 to sustain neuronal function essential for viability.
evidence: This is inferred from the synthetic lethality of CaV1-CaV2 and RyR-CaV2 double mutants, but viability of CaV1-RyR double mutants.

claim: CaV1(Δns) animals move slower than wild-type animals.
source: CaV1(Δns) worms moved slower than wild-type worms, and consequently travelled shorter distances during the observation period.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral tracking experiments showing reduced speed in CaV1(Δns) animals.

claim: CaV1(Δns) animals reverse more frequently than wild-type animals.
source: Additionally, CaV1(Δns) worms reversed more frequently, had shorter durations of forward movement, and moved forward shorter distances than wild type (Figure 1C–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral tracking experiments.

claim: CaV1(Δns) animals have shorter durations of forward movement than wild-type animals.
source: Additionally, CaV1(Δns) worms reversed more frequently, had shorter durations of forward movement, and moved forward shorter distances than wild type (Figure 1C–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral tracking experiments.

claim: The speed of locomotion is dependent on CaV1 function in the nervous system.
source: These results indicate that the speed of locomotion is dependent on CaV1 function in the nervous system, and that CaV1 also biases the bistable locomotory circuit toward forward locomotion (Zheng et al., 1999).
evidence: This is inferred from behavioral rescue experiments showing that neuronal expression of CaV1 restores locomotion speed.

claim: CaV1 biases the bistable locomotory circuit toward forward locomotion.
source: These results indicate that the speed of locomotion is dependent on CaV1 function in the nervous system, and that CaV1 also biases the bistable locomotory circuit toward forward locomotion (Zheng et al., 1999).
evidence: This is inferred from the increased reversal frequency in CaV1(Δns) animals and supported by prior knowledge of the locomotory circuit.

claim: The rate of miniature postsynaptic currents is significantly reduced in CaV2 mutants compared to wild type.
source: The rate of miniature postsynaptic currents (minis/s) compared to the wild type (32.2+/-2.1 minis/s) was significantly reduced in each of the single mutants, CaV2 (18.7+/-3.5 minis/s), CaV1(Δns) (18.7+/-3.6 minis/s), and RyR (20.9+/-1.5 minis/s) (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The rate of miniature postsynaptic currents is significantly reduced in CaV1(Δns) mutants compared to wild type.
source: The rate of miniature postsynaptic currents (minis/s) compared to the wild type (32.2+/-2.1 minis/s) was significantly reduced in each of the single mutants, CaV2 (18.7+/-3.5 minis/s), CaV1(Δns) (18.7+/-3.6 minis/s), and RyR (20.9+/-1.5 minis/s) (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The rate of miniature postsynaptic currents is significantly reduced in RyR mutants compared to wild type.
source: The rate of miniature postsynaptic currents (minis/s) compared to the wild type (32.2+/-2.1 minis/s) was significantly reduced in each of the single mutants, CaV2 (18.7+/-3.5 minis/s), CaV1(Δns) (18.7+/-3.6 minis/s), and RyR (20.9+/-1.5 minis/s) (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Nemadipine is an effective blocker of CaV1 and does not block CaV2.
source: These data demonstrate that nemadipine is an effective blocker of CaV1 and does not block CaV2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology showing that nemadipine reduces minis in wild type to the same level as CaV1(Δns) mutants, and does not further reduce minis in CaV1(Δns) mutants.

claim: Nemadipine application in the RyR mutant does not exacerbate the phenotype.
source: Nemadipine application in the RyR mutant did not exacerbate the phenotype ('RyR(-)+nema', 20.7+/-1.3 mini/s), indicating that CaV1 and RyR function is coupled at neuromuscular junctions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings showing no additive effect of nemadipine in RyR mutants.

claim: CaV1 and RyR function is coupled at neuromuscular junctions.
source: Nemadipine application in the RyR mutant did not exacerbate the phenotype ('RyR(-)+nema', 20.7+/-1.3 mini/s), indicating that CaV1 and RyR function is coupled at neuromuscular junctions.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of additive effect when blocking CaV1 in RyR mutants.

claim: Application of nemadipine almost completely abolishes mini frequency in the CaV2 mutant.
source: Application of nemadipine almost completely abolished mini frequency in the CaV2 mutant (+nema 1.7+/-0.6 mini/s).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: All vesicle fusion at neuromuscular junctions relies on CaV1 and CaV2, each contributing about half of the minis.
source: We conclude that all vesicle fusion at neuromuscular junctions relies on CaV1 and CaV2, each contributing about half of the minis, in agreement with an earlier study (Tong et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from electrophysiology showing that blocking both channels eliminates nearly all minis, and each channel contributes approximately equally.

claim: Calcium influx through CaV1 is not sufficient for vesicle fusion; CaV1 relies on internal calcium stores released by RyR to fuse synaptic vesicles.
source: In addition, calcium influx through CaV1 is not sufficient for vesicle fusion; CaV1 relies on internal calcium stores released by RyR to fuse synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that blocking RyR eliminates CaV1-mediated vesicle fusion.

claim: The rate of minis in the CaV1(Δns) RyR double mutant is similar to the single CaV1(Δns) and RyR mutants.
source: We found that the rate of minis in the CaV1(Δns) RyR double mutant (19.6+/-2 mini/s) was similar to the single CaV1(Δns) and RyR mutants, supporting the hypothesis that CaV1 relies on coupling to RyR to activate neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings showing no additive effect in the double mutant.

claim: CaV1 relies on coupling to RyR to activate neurotransmitter release.
source: We found that the rate of minis in the CaV1(Δns) RyR double mutant (19.6+/-2 mini/s) was similar to the single CaV1(Δns) and RyR mutants, supporting the hypothesis that CaV1 relies on coupling to RyR to activate neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of additive effect in the CaV1 RyR double mutant.

claim: CaV1 and RyR are interdependent and act in parallel to CaV2.
source: In summary, these results demonstrate that CaV1 and RyR are interdependent, and act in parallel to CaV2.
evidence: This is inferred from genetic interaction studies and electrophysiology showing that CaV1 and RyR function together, and their combined function is parallel to CaV2.

claim: Dantrolene is a specific RyR inhibitor.
source: To confirm that the reduction of minis observed in the unc-68 null mutant was due to an acute loss of RyR function rather than a developmental defect, we blocked RyR by applying dantrolene (10 µM), a specific RyR inhibitor (Song et al., 1993; Xu et al., 2001), either alone or in combination with the CaV1 blocker nemadipine.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The frequency of minis is reduced by dantrolene treatment compared to wild type.
source: The frequency of minis was reduced in all treatments compared to the wild type (Figure 2C; wild type 21.7±1.0 mini/s; dantrolene alone 12.36+/-0.6 mini/s; nemadipine alone 15.8+/-0.7 mini/s; dantrolene plus nemadipine 12.2+/-0.9 mini/s).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Nemadipine does not exacerbate the inhibitory effect of dantrolene on minis.
source: Furthermore, nemadipine did not exacerbate the inhibitory effect of dantrolene on minis. Again, CaV1 is reliant on RyR for neurotransmission.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings showing no additive effect of nemadipine when combined with dantrolene.

claim: RyR acts presynaptically to regulate minis.
source: Previously, we rescued minis in a null mutant by expressing wild-type unc-68 in neurons but not muscle cells, suggesting that RyRs regulate minis by acting presynaptically (Liu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by prior rescue experiments cited in the text.

claim: The frequency of minis is significantly reduced in RyR(Δns) compared to wild type.
source: The frequency of minis was significantly reduced compared to the wild type (wild type 21.7±1.0 mini/s; RyR(Δns) 15.9±0.6 mini/s; p=0.001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The reduction in minis in RyR(Δns) supports the conclusion that RyR is required presynaptically for normal levels of synaptic vesicle fusion.
source: The reduction in minis in RyR(Δns) supports the conclusion that RyR is required presynaptically for normal levels of synaptic vesicle fusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that neuronal-specific loss of RyR reduces minis.

claim: The modal value of miniature currents is similar in all strains tested.
source: Using recording conditions in which only acetylcholine currents are detected, the modal value of miniature currents was similar in all strains (wild type 8 pA, CaV1 block nemadipine 7 pA, RyR block dantrolene 5 pA, CaV1 +RyR block nemadipine +dantrolene 6 pA, RyR(Δns) 6 pA), suggesting that the receptor field is similar for most single vesicle fusions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings and analysis of mini amplitudes.

claim: The receptor field is similar for most single vesicle fusions across different genotypes.
source: Using recording conditions in which only acetylcholine currents are detected, the modal value of miniature currents was similar in all strains (wild type 8 pA, CaV1 block nemadipine 7 pA, RyR block dantrolene 5 pA, CaV1 +RyR block nemadipine +dantrolene 6 pA, RyR(Δns) 6 pA), suggesting that the receptor field is similar for most single vesicle fusions.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar modal amplitudes across genotypes.

claim: The mean current amplitude from acetylcholine release is significantly reduced by pharmacological or genetic block of RyR in neurons.
source: The mean current amplitude from acetylcholine release was significantly reduced by pharmacological or genetic block of RyR in neurons (wild type:12.4±0.6 pA; dantrolene: 8.0±0.3 pA; RyR(Δns): 9.5±0.4 pA) (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The presence of large current events is not reduced by mutation of CaV2.
source: The presence of large current events was not reduced by mutation of CaV2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of mini amplitude distributions in CaV2 mutants.

claim: Block of CaV1 by nemadipine causes a decrease in the mean current amplitude.
source: Block of CaV1 by nemadipine caused a decrease in the mean current amplitude (wild type:12.4±0.6 pA; nemadipine: 10.1±0.6 pA; nemadipine +dantrolene: 8.2±0.24 pA), suggesting that CaV1 contributes to multiquantal release.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: CaV1 contributes to multiquantal release.
source: Block of CaV1 by nemadipine caused a decrease in the mean current amplitude (wild type:12.4±0.6 pA; nemadipine: 10.1±0.6 pA; nemadipine +dantrolene: 8.2±0.24 pA), suggesting that CaV1 contributes to multiquantal release.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduction in mean amplitude when CaV1 is blocked.

claim: CaV1 is functionally coupled to RyR to drive multiquantal release.
source: Together, these data indicate that CaV1 is coupled to the ryanodine receptor at synapses to drive multiquantal release.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that blocking either CaV1 or RyR reduces multiquantal release.

claim: CaV2 is functionally coupled to RyR to drive multiquantal release in acetylcholine motor neurons.
source: CaV2 is also functionally coupled to RyR to drive multiquantal release in acetylcholine motor neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology showing that blocking RyR reduces the amplitude of CaV2-mediated minis.

claim: Mini amplitudes arising solely from CaV2 are reduced by blocking RyR.
source: When CaV1 channels are blocked by nemadipine, the remaining miniature currents rely on CaV2 and RyR (Figure 2D), and mini amplitudes arising solely from CaV2 were reduced by further blocking RyR (nemadipine: 10.1+/-0.6 pA; dantrolene +nemadipine: 8.2+/-0.24 pA), suggesting that RyR also responds to calcium from CaV2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: RyR responds to calcium from CaV2.
source: When CaV1 channels are blocked by nemadipine, the remaining miniature currents rely on CaV2 and RyR (Figure 2D), and mini amplitudes arising solely from CaV2 were reduced by further blocking RyR (nemadipine: 10.1+/-0.6 pA; dantrolene +nemadipine: 8.2+/-0.24 pA), suggesting that RyR also responds to calcium from CaV2.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduction in CaV2-mediated mini amplitudes when RyR is blocked.

claim: In the presence of CaV2 and RyR, 34% of currents are multiquantal.
source: In the presence of CaV2 and RyR 34% of currents are multiquantal; blocking RyR reduces multiquantal release to 25% (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is calculated from quantal analysis of mini amplitude distributions.

claim: Blocking RyR reduces multiquantal release to 25%.
source: In the presence of CaV2 and RyR 34% of currents are multiquantal; blocking RyR reduces multiquantal release to 25% (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is calculated from quantal analysis of mini amplitude distributions.

claim: RyR contributes to CaV2-mediated vesicle fusion by enhancing multiquantal events.
source: These fits indicate that RyR contributes to CaV2-mediated vesicle fusion by enhancing multiquantal events, though multiquantal events can also be attributed to CaV2.
evidence: This is inferred from quantal analysis showing that RyR increases the proportion of multiquantal events.

claim: CaV2 and CaV1 channels regulate the release of separate synaptic vesicle pools at neuromuscular junctions.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that CaV2 and CaV1 channels regulate the release of separate synaptic vesicle pools at neuromuscular junctions.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology, electron microscopy, and super-resolution imaging data.

claim: CaV1 requires the ryanodine receptor for any vesicle fusion.
source: CaV1 requires the ryanodine receptor for any vesicle fusion, consistent with the known relationship of these channels in calcium-activated calcium release.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology and electron microscopy showing no CaV1-mediated fusion in RyR mutants.

claim: Calcium influx through CaV2 is sufficient to fuse vesicles on its own.
source: Calcium influx through CaV2 is sufficient to fuse vesicles on its own, although neurotransmitter release is amplified by calcium release from internal stores via the ryanodine receptor.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology showing that CaV2 can mediate vesicle fusion in the absence of RyR, though at reduced amplitude.

claim: Neurotransmitter release mediated by CaV2 is amplified by calcium release from internal stores via the ryanodine receptor.
source: Calcium influx through CaV2 is sufficient to fuse vesicles on its own, although neurotransmitter release is amplified by calcium release from internal stores via the ryanodine receptor.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology showing increased mini amplitudes when RyR is present.

claim: Docked vesicles are defined as those in contact with the plasma membrane in electron microscopy analysis.
source: Docked vesicles were defined as those in contact with the plasma membrane; docking was scored blind to treatment and genotype (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is a methodological definition used in the electron microscopy analysis.

claim: Decreases in docked vesicles after stimulation are assumed to be the result of synaptic vesicle fusion.
source: Decreases in docked vesicles after stimulation were assumed to be the result of synaptic vesicle fusion, although calcium influx could cause some vesicles to undock and return to the cytoplasm (Kusick et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an assumption made in the analysis, with acknowledgment of an alternative possibility supported by citation.

claim: Docked vesicles are uniformly depleted after stimulation in wild-type animals.
source: Docked vesicles were uniformly depleted after stimulation in wild-type animals (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy analysis.

claim: In mutants lacking CaV2 channels, docked vesicles are selectively retained adjacent to the dense projection.
source: In mutants lacking CaV2 channels, docked vesicles were selectively retained adjacent to the dense projection, but fused normally in regions distal from the dense projection.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy analysis showing spatial patterns of vesicle fusion in CaV2 mutants.

claim: In mutants lacking CaV2 channels, vesicles fuse normally in regions distal from the dense projection.
source: In mutants lacking CaV2 channels, docked vesicles were selectively retained adjacent to the dense projection, but fused normally in regions distal from the dense projection.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy analysis.

claim: CaV2 is essential for vesicle fusion at sites adjacent to the dense projection.
source: These results indicate that CaV2 is essential for vesicle fusion at sites adjacent to the dense projection (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is inferred from the selective retention of docked vesicles adjacent to the dense projection in CaV2 mutants.

claim: Mutation of the CaV1 channel reduces fusion broadly.
source: Mutation of the CaV1 channel reduced fusion broadly, although significant vesicle fusions were observed within 100 nm of the dense projection (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy analysis showing reduced fusion across multiple zones in CaV1 mutants.

claim: In the absence of RyR, only CaV2 is functional.
source: In the absence of RyR only CaV2 is functional, and vesicle fusions were only observed in the 33 nm pool — directly adjacent to the dense projection (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RyR mutants only show fusion adjacent to the dense projection, where CaV2 is located.

claim: In RyR mutants, vesicle fusions are only observed in the 33 nm pool directly adjacent to the dense projection.
source: In the absence of RyR only CaV2 is functional, and vesicle fusions were only observed in the 33 nm pool — directly adjacent to the dense projection (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy analysis.

claim: The CaV1 CaV2 double mutant exhibits no change in the number and distribution of docked synaptic vesicles after stimulation.
source: The CaV1 CaV2 double mutant exhibited no change in the number and distribution of docked synaptic vesicles after stimulation (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy analysis showing no vesicle fusion in the double mutant.

claim: Baseline docking is increased in the 0–33 nm bin in CaV2(-) mutants.
source: Baseline docking was increased in the 0–33 nm bin in the CaV2(-) mutants, this trend is consistent with decreased tonic fusion adjacent to the dense projection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and release probability of vesicles is reduced adjacent to the dense projection in CaV2(-) mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy analysis.

claim: Release probability of vesicles is reduced adjacent to the dense projection in CaV2(-) mutants.
source: Baseline docking was increased in the 0–33 nm bin in the CaV2(-) mutants, this trend is consistent with decreased tonic fusion adjacent to the dense projection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and release probability of vesicles is reduced adjacent to the dense projection in CaV2(-) mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is calculated from electron microscopy data.

claim: Identical fusion defects are observed in the intermediate zone in the CaV2(-) mutant and RyR(-) mutant.
source: However, we observed identical fusion defects in the intermediate zone in the CaV2(-) mutant and RyR(-) mutant, which suggests CaV2 activates RyR to release calcium from internal stores.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy analysis showing similar fusion patterns in both mutants.

claim: CaV2 activates RyR to release calcium from internal stores.
source: However, we observed identical fusion defects in the intermediate zone in the CaV2(-) mutant and RyR(-) mutant, which suggests CaV2 activates RyR to release calcium from internal stores.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar fusion defects in CaV2 and RyR mutants in the intermediate zone.

claim: Activation of RyR by CaV2 is consistent with the multiquantal release mediated by these channels.
source: Activation of RyR by CaV2 is consistent with the multiquantal release mediated by these channels (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between RyR activation and multiquantal release observed in electrophysiology.

claim: The probability of vesicle fusion in the distal active zone is reduced in CaV1(-) mutants.
source: In the distal active zone (165–594 nm), the probability of vesicle fusion was reduced in CaV1(-) mutants, RyR(-) mutants, and CaV2(-) CaV1(-) double mutants, but slightly increased in CaV2(-) mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is calculated from electron microscopy data.

claim: The probability of vesicle fusion in the distal active zone is reduced in RyR(-) mutants.
source: In the distal active zone (165–594 nm), the probability of vesicle fusion was reduced in CaV1(-) mutants, RyR(-) mutants, and CaV2(-) CaV1(-) double mutants, but slightly increased in CaV2(-) mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is calculated from electron microscopy data.

claim: The probability of vesicle fusion in the distal active zone is slightly increased in CaV2(-) mutants.
source: In the distal active zone (165–594 nm), the probability of vesicle fusion was reduced in CaV1(-) mutants, RyR(-) mutants, and CaV2(-) CaV1(-) double mutants, but slightly increased in CaV2(-) mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is calculated from electron microscopy data.

claim: An increase in fusion at distal sites in CaV2 mutants might be due to compensatory effects in the expression or organization of CaV1 and RyR.
source: An increase in fusion at distal sites in CaV2 mutants might be due to compensatory effects in the expression or organization of CaV1 and RyR.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed increase in distal fusion in CaV2 mutants.

claim: CaV2 mediates fusion of vesicles adjacent to the dense projection.
source: Together, electron microscopy indicates that CaV2 mediates fusion of vesicles adjacent to the dense projection, and that CaV1 mediates fusion of vesicles at lateral sites.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy showing spatial patterns of vesicle fusion in calcium channel mutants.

claim: CaV1 mediates fusion of vesicles at lateral sites.
source: Together, electron microscopy indicates that CaV2 mediates fusion of vesicles adjacent to the dense projection, and that CaV1 mediates fusion of vesicles at lateral sites.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy showing spatial patterns of vesicle fusion in calcium channel mutants.

claim: The ryanodine receptor is essential for vesicle fusion mediated by CaV1 at lateral sites.
source: The ryanodine receptor is essential for vesicle fusion mediated by CaV1 at lateral sites and contributes to vesicle fusion by CaV2 near the dense projection.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy showing no lateral fusion in RyR mutants.

claim: The ryanodine receptor contributes to vesicle fusion by CaV2 near the dense projection.
source: The ryanodine receptor is essential for vesicle fusion mediated by CaV1 at lateral sites and contributes to vesicle fusion by CaV2 near the dense projection.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy showing reduced fusion in the intermediate zone in RyR mutants.

claim: Dense projections at neuromuscular junctions are spaced roughly 1 µm apart in electron microscopy reconstruction.
source: Dense projections at neuromuscular junctions were spaced roughly 1 µm apart in the reconstruction (1.02 / µm).
evidence: This is measured from electron microscopy reconstruction of the dorsal nerve cord.

claim: The distribution of CaV2 clusters along the dorsal cord matches the spacing of dense projections.
source: This matches well to the distribution of CaV2 clusters (1.10+/-0.16 µm) along the dorsal cord by super-resolution microscopy, and is consistent with previous studies demonstrating that CaV2 /UNC-2 channels are localized to dense projections by immuno-electron microscopy (Gracheva et al., 2008).
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution microscopy and supported by prior immuno-EM studies.

claim: CaV2 is localized to the dense projection.
source: To further demonstrate that CaV2 is localized to the dense projection, we compared CaV2 localization with CRISPR-tagged presynaptic active zone proteins, including Neurexin (nrx-1), Magi (magi-1), SYDE (syd-1), Liprin-α (syd-2), RIMBP (rimb-1), and α-Catulin (ctn-1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution microscopy showing colocalization with dense projection markers.

claim: CaV2 colocalizes with all tested active zone proteins.
source: CaV2 colocalized with all these proteins (Figure 4B), indicating that it is indeed localized at the dense projection.
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution microscopy.

claim: ELKS clusters are tightly associated with CaV2 clusters.
source: ELKS clusters in particular are tightly associated with CaV2 clusters and exhibit the same 1 µm spacing (Figure 4C), and serves as a synaptic fiducial.
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution microscopy showing similar spacing and colocalization.

claim: CaV2 clusters and ELKS clusters are similar in diameter (297 nm vs 294 nm, respectively).
source: CaV2 clusters and ELKS clusters were similar in diameter (297 nm vs 294 nm, respectively, n=26 synapses).
evidence: This is measured from super-resolution microscopy data.

claim: The cluster centers of CaV2 and ELKS are slightly offset (124 nm).
source: The cluster centers are slightly offset (Ᾱ=124 nm), so that 62% of ELKS localizations were within a CaV2 cluster (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is measured from super-resolution microscopy data.

claim: 62% of ELKS localizations are within a CaV2 cluster.
source: The cluster centers are slightly offset (Ᾱ=124 nm), so that 62% of ELKS localizations were within a CaV2 cluster (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is calculated from super-resolution microscopy data.

claim: The offset between CaV2 and ELKS clusters could indicate that the clusters overlap but are not coincident.
source: The offset could indicate that the clusters overlap but are not coincident. Alternatively, these proteins may be perfectly colocalized but differ in our plots due to the positions of the tags on the proteins; specifically, CaV2 was tagged on the extracellular side in the synaptic cleft, whereas ELKS was tagged at the C-terminus on the intracellular side.
evidence: This is speculation about the interpretation of the observed offset.

claim: CaV2 and ELKS may be perfectly colocalized but differ in localization plots due to the positions of the tags on the proteins.
source: The offset could indicate that the clusters overlap but are not coincident. Alternatively, these proteins may be perfectly colocalized but differ in our plots due to the positions of the tags on the proteins; specifically, CaV2 was tagged on the extracellular side in the synaptic cleft, whereas ELKS was tagged at the C-terminus on the intracellular side.
evidence: This is speculation about the interpretation of the observed offset based on knowledge of protein structure and tagging strategy.

claim: CaV2 is tightly clustered and associated with an ELKS cluster.
source: In summary, CaV2 is tightly clustered and associated with an ELKS cluster; the offset may simply be due to tagging sites and the length of the proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from super-resolution microscopy data showing colocalization and similar cluster dimensions.

claim: CaV1 is broadly distributed as dispersed puncta in the synaptic bouton with a cluster diameter of 869 nm.
source: In contrast to CaV2, CaV1 was broadly distributed as dispersed puncta in the synaptic bouton ('cluster' diameter 869 nm), and is largely excluded from ELKS and CaV2 clusters (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is measured from super-resolution microscopy data.

claim: CaV1 is largely excluded from ELKS and CaV2 clusters.
source: In contrast to CaV2, CaV1 was broadly distributed as dispersed puncta in the synaptic bouton ('cluster' diameter 869 nm), and is largely excluded from ELKS and CaV2 clusters (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution microscopy showing spatial separation between CaV1 and CaV2/ELKS.

claim: CaV1 usually exhibits a site of high density that is about 250 nm from the ELKS and CaV2 clusters.
source: Although dispersed, CaV1 usually exhibits a site of high density that is about 250 nm from the ELKS and CaV2 clusters (262 nm and 274 nm, respectively; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is measured from super-resolution microscopy data.

claim: CaV1 clusters often abut CaV2 clusters.
source: Although CaV1 is largely excluded from CaV2 clusters, the clusters often abut one another (Figure 5B, see Figure 10 for more examples).
evidence: This is observed in super-resolution microscopy images.

claim: The overexpressed CaV1::HALO tends to be more punctate than the endogenously tagged protein.
source: The overexpressed CaV1::HALO tended to be more punctate than the endogenously tagged protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is observed by comparing super-resolution images of endogenous and overexpressed CaV1.

claim: CaV1 does not colocalize with RIMBP.
source: CaV1 did not colocalize with RIMBP and the mean distance to the dense projection was similar to the endogenously tagged gene (endogenous CaV1 to ELKS, 262 nm; transgene CaV1 to RIMBP, 378 nm; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution microscopy.

claim: CaV1 and LIN-7 localizations are overlapping but distal to the dense projection marker RIMBP.
source: CaV1 and LIN-7 localizations were overlapping, but distal to the dense projection marker RIMBP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution microscopy.

claim: CaV1 is localized at presynaptic boutons in a separate domain from CaV2 channels.
source: These data suggest that CaV1 is localized at presynaptic boutons in a separate domain from CaV2 channels.
evidence: This is inferred from super-resolution microscopy showing spatial separation and colocalization with presynaptic markers.

claim: RyR localizations are diffusely distributed and lateral to the dense projection.
source: RyR localizations were diffusely distributed, and lateral to the dense projection (ELKS to RyR center of mass distance: 393 nm; 25 synapses) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is measured from super-resolution microscopy data.

claim: RyR localizations are correlated with CaV1 (RyR to CaV1 center of mass: 166 nm).
source: RyR localizations were correlated with CaV1 (RyR to CaV1 center of mass: 166 nm).
evidence: This is measured from super-resolution microscopy data.

claim: RyR and CaV1 are often interdigitated in adjacent zones.
source: Visual inspection of the images suggested that RyR and CaV1 are often interdigitated in adjacent zones (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is observed in super-resolution microscopy images.

claim: 94% of RyR localizations are within 100 nm of a CaV1 localization.
source: To characterize this relationship a nearest neighbor analysis was performed and revealed that 94% of RyR localizations were within 100 nm of a CaV1 localization (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is calculated from nearest neighbor analysis of super-resolution microscopy data.

claim: 82% of CaV1 localizations are within 100 nm of a RyR channel.
source: CaV1 exhibits a slightly broader distribution; nevertheless, 82% of CaV1 localizations were within 100 nm of a RyR channel.
evidence: This is calculated from nearest neighbor analysis of super-resolution microscopy data.

claim: The spatial correlation between CaV1 and RyR is consistent with the functional coupling observed by physiology and electron microscopy.
source: The spatial correlation between CaV1 and RyR is consistent with the functional coupling observed by physiology and electron microscopy.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between spatial proximity and functional dependence.

claim: Null mutations in unc-13 nearly eliminate neurotransmission and vesicle docking in C. elegans.
source: Null mutations in unc-13 nearly eliminate neurotransmission and vesicle docking in C. elegans (Hammarlund et al., 2007; Richmond et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: In most organisms, there are two types of Unc13 proteins: those with an N-terminal C2A domain and those lacking the C2A domain.
source: In most organisms, there are two types of Unc13 proteins, those with an N-terminal C2A domain, and those lacking the C2A domain (Dittman, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Binding of the C2A domain to the scaffolding protein RIM activates Unc13.
source: Binding of the C2A domain to the scaffolding protein RIM activates Unc13 (Betz et al., 2001; Hu et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2006; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Unc13 isoforms which lack a C2A domain bind ELKS / CAST in flies and mice.
source: Unc13 isoforms which lack a C2A domain bind ELKS / CAST in flies and mice (Böhme et al., 2018; Kawabe et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: In C. elegans, the unc-13 gene encodes two major splice isoforms: UNC-13L with a C2A domain and UNC-13S lacking a C2A domain.
source: In C. elegans, the unc-13 gene encodes two major splice isoforms: a long isoform UNC-13L with a C2A domain, and a short isoform UNC-13S lacking a C2A domain.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of C. elegans gene structure.

claim: Both CaV2 and CaV1 calcium channels are tightly associated with UNC-13 isoforms.
source: Both CaV2 and CaV1 calcium channels were tightly associated with UNC-13 isoforms (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution microscopy.

claim: 99.7% of CaV2 channels are within 100 nm of an UNC-13 localization.
source: Nearest-neighbor analysis indicates that 99.7% of CaV2 channels were within 100 nm of an UNC-13 localization, and 89% of CaV1 channels were within 100 nm of an UNC-13 protein (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is calculated from nearest neighbor analysis of super-resolution microscopy data.

claim: 89% of CaV1 channels are within 100 nm of an UNC-13 protein.
source: Nearest-neighbor analysis indicates that 99.7% of CaV2 channels were within 100 nm of an UNC-13 localization, and 89% of CaV1 channels were within 100 nm of an UNC-13 protein (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is calculated from nearest neighbor analysis of super-resolution microscopy data.

claim: UNC-13S does not colocalize with CaV2 (peak-to-peak 319 nm).
source: UNC-13S did not colocalize with CaV2 (peak-to-peak 319 nm) but was associated with CaV1 (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is measured from super-resolution microscopy data.

claim: UNC-13S is associated with CaV1.
source: UNC-13S did not colocalize with CaV2 (peak-to-peak 319 nm) but was associated with CaV1 (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution microscopy.

claim: 99% of UNC-13S localizations are within 100 nm of a CaV1 channel.
source: Nearest neighbor analysis indicates that 99% of UNC-13S localizations are within 100 nm of a CaV1 channel (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is calculated from nearest neighbor analysis of super-resolution microscopy data.

claim: CaV1 channels are associated with UNC-13S at lateral sites.
source: These data demonstrate that CaV1 channels are associated with UNC-13S at lateral sites.
evidence: This is inferred from super-resolution microscopy showing colocalization of CaV1 and UNC-13S away from the dense projection.

claim: UNC-13S can dock vesicles independent of UNC-13L.
source: Although it is possible that UNC-13L is also at these lateral sites, UNC-13S can dock vesicles independent of UNC-13L.
evidence: This is supported by prior studies showing that UNC-13S can rescue docking in the absence of UNC-13L.

claim: Rescue of unc-13 null animals with UNC-13S restores locomotion and mini frequency to about half of wild-type.
source: Rescue of unc-13 null animals with UNC-13S restores locomotion and mini frequency to about half of wild-type (Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Mutants lacking UNC-13L have normal or elevated numbers of docked vesicles in lateral regions of the synapse.
source: In contrast to the null, mutants lacking UNC-13L have normal or elevated numbers of docked vesicles in lateral regions of the synapse (Hammarlund et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2013), indicating that the UNC-13S isoform is capable of docking synaptic vesicles in the absence of UNC-13L (Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The UNC-13S isoform is capable of docking synaptic vesicles in the absence of UNC-13L.
source: In contrast to the null, mutants lacking UNC-13L have normal or elevated numbers of docked vesicles in lateral regions of the synapse (Hammarlund et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2013), indicating that the UNC-13S isoform is capable of docking synaptic vesicles in the absence of UNC-13L (Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that docking is maintained in lateral regions in UNC-13L mutants.

claim: UNC-13L is coupled to CaV2 at the dense projection.
source: Together, the localization data, electron microscopy, and physiology indicate that UNC-13L is coupled to CaV2 at the dense projection, and UNC-13S is coupled to CaV1 and the ryanodine receptor at lateral sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing colocalization and functional coupling.

claim: UNC-13S is coupled to CaV1 and the ryanodine receptor at lateral sites.
source: Together, the localization data, electron microscopy, and physiology indicate that UNC-13L is coupled to CaV2 at the dense projection, and UNC-13S is coupled to CaV1 and the ryanodine receptor at lateral sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing colocalization and functional coupling.

claim: Both CaV2 and CaV1 channels drive vesicle fusion at C. elegans neuromuscular junctions.
source: Here, we demonstrate that both CaV2 and CaV1 channels drive vesicle fusion at C. elegans neuromuscular junctions and mediate the release of different synaptic vesicle pools.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology, electron microscopy, and super-resolution imaging.

claim: CaV2 channels fuse vesicles near the dense projection at the center of the synapse.
source: Flash-and-freeze electron microscopy revealed that CaV2 channels fuse vesicles near the dense projection at the center of the synapse; whereas CaV1 channels fuse vesicles at lateral sites in the same synapses.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flash-and-freeze electron microscopy.

claim: CaV1 channels fuse vesicles at lateral sites in the same synapses.
source: Flash-and-freeze electron microscopy revealed that CaV2 channels fuse vesicles near the dense projection at the center of the synapse; whereas CaV1 channels fuse vesicles at lateral sites in the same synapses.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flash-and-freeze electron microscopy.

claim: CaV2 channels are compacted at the dense projection into 250 nm clusters along with active zone proteins ELKS, neurexin, α-Liprin, and RIMBP.
source: Super-resolution imaging indicates that CaV2 channels are compacted at the dense projection into 250 nm clusters, along with the active zone proteins ELKS, neurexin, α-Liprin, and RIMBP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution microscopy.

claim: CaV2 is associated with the long isoform of the docking and priming protein UNC-13L.
source: CaV2 is associated with the long isoform of the docking and priming protein UNC-13L.
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution microscopy showing colocalization.

claim: CaV1 is dispersed in the synaptic varicosity and is associated with the short isoform UNC-13S.
source: By contrast, CaV1 is dispersed in the synaptic varicosity and is associated with the short isoform UNC-13S.
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution microscopy.

claim: Participation of multiple classes of calcium channels at the same synapse may serve to tune the dynamics of neurotransmission.
source: Participation of multiple classes of calcium channels at the same synapse may serve to tune the dynamics of neurotransmission (Dolphin, 2021).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Different calcium sources could regulate the strength of output, dynamics of release, or even termination of synaptic activity.
source: Different calcium sources could regulate the strength of output, dynamics of release, or even termination of synaptic activity.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional implications of multiple calcium channel types.

claim: The number of CaV1 channels per synapse is estimated to be 77±15.
source: The number of CaV1 channels was calculated from the mean number of blinks per channel, as well as from the total photon flux, converging on 77±15 CaV1 channels per synapse (Figure 10B–E).
evidence: This is calculated from single molecule localization microscopy data using two independent methods.

claim: The number of RyR channels per synapse is estimated to be 29±4.
source: Using the mean blinks per channel produces an estimate of 29±4 RYR channels per synapse (Figure 10G).
evidence: This is calculated from single molecule localization microscopy data.

claim: The CaV2 cluster contains approximately 101±16 channels.
source: However, assuming the blinking rate of rhodamine dyes is similar to cyanine dyes (Helmerich et al., 2022), the frequency of blinking indicates that the cluster contains 101±16 CaV2 channels.
evidence: This is estimated from single molecule localization microscopy data based on assumptions about dye blinking rates.

claim: The ~100 CaV2 channels per synapse is much higher than the ~35 CaV2.1 channels determined by immunogold labelling synapses in the mouse central nervous system.
source: The ~100 CaV2 channels per synapse derived from our single molecule localization data is much higher than the ~35 CaV2.1 channels determined by immunogold labelling synapses in the mouse central nervous system (Holderith et al., 2012; Kusch et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior studies in mammalian systems.

claim: The density of calcium channels at C. elegans neuromuscular junctions (91 CaV2 per µm2) is similar to mammalian synapses (100–400 CaV2.1 channels per µm2).
source: Nevertheless, the density of calcium channels at C. elegans neuromuscular junctions (91 CaV2 per µm2) is similar to mammalian synapses (100–400 CaV2.1 channels per µm2).
evidence: This is calculated from the channel counts and synapse dimensions, and compared to literature values.

claim: A large number of channels is required because single calcium channels open stochastically and can introduce jitter to the precise timing of a signal.
source: A large number of channels is required because single calcium channels open stochastically, and can introduce jitter to the precise timing of a signal (Borst and Sakmann, 1996).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of calcium channel biophysics supported by citation.

claim: For synapses to reliably track high frequency action potentials, there must be a sufficient number of channels to ensure that some open immediately in response to depolarization.
source: For synapses to reliably track high frequency action potentials, there must be a sufficient number of channels to insure that some open immediately in response to depolarization.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of synaptic physiology.

claim: A dense cluster of CaV2 channels will promote a rapid synaptic response to rapid depolarizations.
source: Nematode motor neurons rely on graded potentials rather than conventional action potentials; nevertheless, a dense cluster of CaV2 channels will promote a rapid synaptic response to rapid depolarizations.
evidence: This is inferred from the properties of dense channel clusters and knowledge of synaptic physiology.

claim: The docked synaptic vesicle must be just 20–30 nm from the calcium channel for the calcium concentration in the nanodomain to be high enough to drive vesicle fusion.
source: The calcium channels must be physically coupled to the neurotransmitter release site, that is, the docked synaptic vesicle must be just 20–30 nm from the calcium channel, for the calcium concentration in the nanodomain to be high enough to drive vesicle fusion (Fedchyshyn and Wang, 2005; Weber et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of calcium nanodomain dynamics supported by citations.

claim: At C. elegans neuromuscular junctions, UNC-13L mediates tight coupling (EGTA-insensitive).
source: At C. elegans neuromuscular junctions, UNC-13L mediates tight coupling (EGTA-insensitive), whereas UNC-13S mediates loose coupling (EGTA-sensitive) (Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: UNC-13S mediates loose coupling (EGTA-sensitive).
source: At C. elegans neuromuscular junctions, UNC-13L mediates tight coupling (EGTA-insensitive), whereas UNC-13S mediates loose coupling (EGTA-sensitive) (Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: UNC-13L is colocalized with CaV2 at dense projections.
source: Here, we found that UNC-13L is colocalized with CaV2 at dense projections.
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution microscopy.

claim: CaV2 mediates the release of vesicles within 33 nm of the dense projection, consistent with EGTA-insensitive priming by UNC-13L.
source: Consistent with EGTA-insensitive priming by UNC-13L, CaV2 mediates the release of vesicles within 33 nm of the dense projection (Hammarlund et al., 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy and supported by citation to prior work on UNC-13L.

claim: The dense cluster of CaV2 channels transfers enough calcium from the synaptic cleft to fuse multiple vesicles upon depolarization.
source: Finally, the dense cluster of CaV2 channels transfers enough calcium from the synaptic cleft to fuse multiple vesicles upon depolarization – termed multiquantal release.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of multiquantal release in electrophysiology experiments.

claim: The calcium influx from CaV2 activates the ryanodine receptor, which drives fusion of vesicles docked beyond 33 nm in the intermediate active zone (33–165 nm).
source: The calcium influx from CaV2 also activates the ryanodine receptor, which in turn drives fusion of vesicles docked beyond 33 nm in the intermediate active zone (33–165 nm).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy showing fusion patterns in the intermediate zone.

claim: The frequency of CaV2-mediated fusion is not affected by presence or loss of RyR.
source: The frequency of CaV2-mediated fusion is not affected by presence or loss of RyR, indicating that CaV2 reliably drives vesicle fusion in response to depolarizations on its own.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology showing similar mini frequencies in the presence or absence of RyR when only CaV2 is functional.

claim: Only the amplitude of CaV2-mediated currents is reduced in the absence of RyR.
source: Only the amplitude of these currents is reduced in the absence of RyR, indicating that the ryanodine receptor only potentiates CaV2 responses by releasing calcium from internal stores.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology showing reduced mini amplitudes but not frequency when RyR is blocked.

claim: The ryanodine receptor only potentiates CaV2 responses by releasing calcium from internal stores.
source: Only the amplitude of these currents is reduced in the absence of RyR, indicating that the ryanodine receptor only potentiates CaV2 responses by releasing calcium from internal stores.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RyR affects amplitude but not frequency of CaV2-mediated minis.

claim: The ryanodine receptor is activated by low levels of cytosolic calcium and releases calcium from internal stores.
source: In contrast to CaV2, CaV1 localizations are dispersed broadly in the synapse and localizations are frequently solitary. Calcium influx mediated by CaV1 is not sufficient to drive vesicle fusion directly, but the ryanodine receptor is activated by low levels of cytosolic calcium and releases calcium from internal stores.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of ryanodine receptor function.

claim: Two-step calcium signaling via CaV1 and RyR is consistent with the EGTA-sensitivity of UNC-13S vesicle fusion.
source: Two-step calcium signaling is consistent with the EGTA-sensitivity of UNC-13S vesicle fusion (Hu et al., 2013); EGTA can buffer the small amount of calcium from CaV1 before it detonates the ryanodine receptor, or buffer calcium diffusing from the endoplasmic reticulum to the UNC-13S docking site.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between two-step signaling and EGTA sensitivity, supported by citation.

claim: CaV1 channels inactivate slowly and are more responsive to long duration synaptic depolarizations.
source: CaV1 channels inactivate slowly (the moniker 'L-type' refers to 'long-lasting') and are therefore more responsive to long duration synaptic depolarizations (Naranjo et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of CaV1 channel biophysics supported by citations.

claim: Slow inactivation of CaV1.3 and CaV1.4 channels allows synapses in sensory neurons to accurately report the depolarization status of the synaptic bouton.
source: For example, slow inactivation of CaV1.3 and CaV1.4 channels allows synapses in sensory neurons to accurately report the depolarization status of the synaptic bouton (McRory et al., 2004; Platzer et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: EGL-19 exhibits slow inactivation.
source: Similarly, EGL-19 exhibits slow inactivation (Lainé et al., 2014), which likely contributes to graded miniature currents at C. elegans synapses (Liu et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Slow inactivation of EGL-19 likely contributes to graded miniature currents at C. elegans synapses.
source: Similarly, EGL-19 exhibits slow inactivation (Lainé et al., 2014), which likely contributes to graded miniature currents at C. elegans synapses (Liu et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is inferred from the properties of EGL-19 and supported by citation.

claim: The miniature currents mediated by RyR are large amplitude currents and are likely to be multiquantal vesicle fusions.
source: The miniature currents mediated by RyR are large amplitude currents, and are likely to be multiquantal vesicle fusions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RyR-mediated minis have larger amplitudes.

claim: The ultimate output of calcium release from internal stores might be a rapid shutdown of synaptic transmission.
source: Despite the potentiation of neurotransmitter release by the ryanodine receptor, the ultimate output of calcium release from internal stores might be a rapid shutdown of synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of RyR.

claim: In CA1 hippocampal neurons, CaV1 channels and RyR2 activate calcium-gated potassium channels in the cell body and hyperpolarize the neuron.
source: In CA1 hippocampal neurons CaV1 channels and RyR2 activate calcium gated-potassium channels in the cell body of mouse CA1 hippocampal neurons and hyperpolarize the neuron (Sahu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: In C. elegans, CaV1 activity is specifically coupled to SLO-2 BK potassium channels.
source: In C. elegans, CaV1 activity is specifically coupled to SLO-2 BK potassium channels (Liu et al., 2014), activation of SLO-2 by a calcium burst would hyperpolarize the membrane and terminate synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Activation of SLO-2 by a calcium burst would hyperpolarize the membrane and terminate synaptic transmission.
source: In C. elegans, CaV1 activity is specifically coupled to SLO-2 BK potassium channels (Liu et al., 2014), activation of SLO-2 by a calcium burst would hyperpolarize the membrane and terminate synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is inferred from knowledge of potassium channel function and supported by citation.

claim: RyR is inhibited by high concentrations of calcium.
source: Furthermore, RyR is inhibited by high concentrations of calcium.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of RyR function.

claim: Hyperpolarization mediated by calcium sparks could act as a safety mechanism to break the positive feedback loop of calcium at synapses.
source: Hyperpolarization mediated by calcium sparks could act as a safety mechanism to break the positive feedback loop of calcium at synapses, or could regulate switching between neuronal circuits.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of calcium-mediated hyperpolarization.

claim: The ryanodine receptor is directly stimulated by calcium binding to the receptor.
source: The ryanodine receptor is directly stimulated by calcium binding to the receptor (des Georges et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Activation of the ryanodine receptor depends on the diffusion rate of calcium, buffering capacity, and the distance between the voltage-gated calcium channel and the ryanodine receptor.
source: Activation of the ryanodine receptor will then depend on the diffusion rate of calcium, buffering capacity, and the distance between the voltage-gated calcium channel and the ryanodine receptor.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of calcium signaling dynamics.

claim: Modeling studies suggest that the endoplasmic reticulum must be within ~100 nm of vesicle, and that high-frequency stimulation may be required to overcome barriers to RyR activation.
source: Modeling studies suggest that the endoplasmic reticulum must be within ~100 nm of vesicle, and that high-frequency stimulation may be required to overcome these barriers (Bouchard et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a modeling study.

claim: The voltage sensor in CaV1 could be physically coupled to RyR and bypass the requirement for calcium diffusion.
source: Alternatively, the voltage sensor in CaV1 could be physically coupled to RyR and bypass the requirement for calcium diffusion.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism for CaV1-RyR coupling.

claim: In skeletal muscle, CaV1.1 is physically coupled to RYR1 and voltage-sensing by the calcium channel can gate the ryanodine receptor in the absence of extracellular calcium.
source: In skeletal muscle, CaV1.1 is physically coupled to RYR1 and voltage-sensing by the calcium channel can gate the ryanodine receptor in the absence of extracellular calcium (Schneider, 1994; Shoshan-Barmatz and Ashley, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: In hippocampal cells, CaV1.3 is physically coupled to RyR2 and depolarization alone is sufficient to release calcium stores.
source: In hippocampal cells, CaV1.3 is physically coupled to RyR2 and depolarization alone is sufficient to release calcium stores (Kim et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: In C. elegans, large amplitude currents were not eliminated in 0 mM extracellular calcium.
source: Similarly, in C. elegans, large amplitude currents were not eliminated in 0 mM extracellular calcium (Liu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: In unc-68(-) mutants, miniature currents were completely eliminated in 0 mM external calcium.
source: But in unc-68(-) mutants, which lack the ryanodine receptor, miniature currents were completely eliminated in 0 mM external calcium (Liu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: In C. elegans, release of calcium from internal stores may be coupled by a physical link to a voltage sensor.
source: These data suggest that in worms, release of calcium from internal stores may also be coupled by a physical link to a voltage sensor.
evidence: This is speculation based on prior observations in C. elegans and other systems.

claim: The invertebrate dense projection comprises many of the proteins associated with the full breadth of the vertebrate synapse.
source: Our data indicate that this structure comprises many of the proteins associated with the full breadth of the vertebrate synapse, including the adhesion molecules Neurexin and SYDE, and the active zone proteins RIMB and ELKS / CAST.
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution microscopy showing colocalization of these proteins at the dense projection.

claim: The vertebrate synapse is not homogenous in organization; CaV2, RIM, Munc13, and Bassoon form irregular clusters in the active zone.
source: Although lacking a focused density, the vertebrate synapse is not homogenous in organization; CaV2, RIM, Munc13, and Bassoon form irregular clusters in the active zone (Holderith et al., 2012; Kawabe et al., 2017; Kusch et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies in vertebrate systems.

claim: The invertebrate dense projection may serve to create a single density of CaV2 channels for synaptic reliability and speed at the sacrifice of synaptic plasticity.
source: The invertebrate dense projection may serve to create a single density of CaV2 channels for synaptic reliability and speed at the sacrifice of synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of the dense projection structure.

claim: CaV1 channels are present at neuromuscular junctions in the fly and mouse.
source: In addition to CaV2 channels, CaV1 channels are also present at neuromuscular junctions in the fly and mouse (Katz et al., 1996; Krick et al., 2021; Urbano and Uchitel, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: CaV1.2 and CaV1.3 are expressed broadly in the brain.
source: CaV1.2 and CaV1.3 are also expressed broadly in the brain (Hell et al., 1996; Hell et al., 1993; Nanou and Catterall, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Pharmacological experiments suggest that CaV2 and CaV1 channels function together in GABA neurons in the central nervous system.
source: Pharmacological experiments suggest that CaV2 and CaV1 channels function together in GABA neurons in the central nervous system.
evidence: This is inferred from prior pharmacological studies.

claim: GABA synapses in the central nervous system depend on both 'tight' and 'loose' coupling to calcium channels as assayed by EGTA.
source: Moreover, these synapses depend on both 'tight' and 'loose' coupling to calcium channels as assayed by EGTA (Eggermann et al., 2011; Goswami et al., 2012; Rey et al., 2020; Vyleta and Jonas, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Ryanodine receptors are found at vertebrate presynapses.
source: CaV1 could also be linked to the release of internal stores in the central nervous system, since ryanodine receptors are found at vertebrate presynapses (Bouchard et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Ryanodine receptors play a role in multiquantal release at inhibitory inputs to Purkinje cells and in hippocampal slice culture.
source: These ryanodine receptors play a role in multiquantal release at inhibitory inputs to Purkinje cells, and in hippocampal slice culture (Llano et al., 2000; Sharma and Vijayaraghavan, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Recruitment of the CaV1-RyR axis would increase neurotransmitter release from synapses.
source: Recruitment of the CaV1-RyR axis would increase neurotransmitter release from these synapses, but ultimately might shut down neurotransmission by activating potassium channels.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of the CaV1-RyR axis.

claim: The tuning of the output of the presynapse depends on the timing and spatial organization of calcium at release sites.
source: The tuning of the output of the presynapse then ultimately depends on the timing and spatial organization of calcium at release sites (Eggermann et al., 2011; Nakamura et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: In C. elegans, calcium channels regulate two separate synaptic vesicle pools distinguished by the docking and priming machinery.
source: In C. elegans, these calcium channels regulate two separate synaptic vesicle pools. It is not known whether the composition of the vesicles in these pools differ, as has been observed in vertebrates (Kavalali, 2015). In C. elegans, these pools are distinguished by the docking and priming machinery: Vesicle docking at CaV2 sites is mediated by UNC-13L; docking to CaV1 sites is mediated by UNC-13S.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the combined data from electron microscopy and super-resolution imaging.

claim: A subset of hippocampal synapses express orthologs of both UNC-13L (Munc13-1) and UNC-13S (bMunc13-2).
source: This organization could be conserved at vertebrate synapses; a subset of hippocampal synapses express orthologs of both UNC-13L (Munc13-1) and UNC-13S (bMunc13-2) (Kawabe et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.
